analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 over six years and ends lower minimums for tipped, teen, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The House passed a $15 federal minimum wage 231-199, but the Senate never voted on it and it expired at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps from the current $7.25 to $15 an hour, and after that adjust it each year with growth in the median American wage so it does not erode. It would also phase out the lower minimum wages that currently apply to tipped workers, newly hired workers under 20, and workers with disabilities, eventually paying all of them the full minimum wage. The House passed it on July 18, 2019; the Senate put it on its calendar and never scheduled a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum or slightly above it, especially in states with no state minimum wage above $7.25. Tipped servers, who could keep their tips and eventually be paid the full minimum by their employer, and workers with disabilities, who would stop being paid a legal subminimum wage.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in annual steps from $8.40 to $15.00 an hour, then adjusts it each year by the growth in the median hourly wage so it keeps pace with typical pay [S5].
Phases out the separate 'tip credit' minimum wage, eventually requiring employers to pay tipped workers the full federal minimum and confirming that employees keep their own tips [S5].

Phases out the lower 'training' minimum for newly hired workers under 20 and the special certificates that let employers pay workers with disabilities below the minimum wage, with federal technical assistance to help those employers transition [S5].

Requires the Labor Department to publish each wage increase at least 60 days before it takes effect, and requires a Government Accountability Office report on the effects of the first increases on businesses, including small businesses [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently pay wages below the new minimum, most heavily restaurants, fast-food chains, retail, and other labor-intensive businesses, along with employers that use the tipped minimum and the disability subminimum certificate program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers, especially restaurants and retail

drawbacks.text: A single national wage floor applies equally in high-cost cities and low-cost rural areas, and critics argued small businesses could not absorb the increase — a House Republican amendment offered on the floor would have exempted businesses with fewer than 10 employees and under $1 million in sales, though the bill already phases increases in over six years [S5].

Eliminating the tipped minimum means restaurant owners must pay servers the full minimum wage directly, a change some restaurant employers argue would lead them to cut hours or shift how servers are paid [S5].

Ending the 14(c) program that lets employers pay workers with disabilities below the minimum wage would close the sheltered-workshop pay model; the bill tries to soften this with transition assistance and by barring only new certificates, but some employers and families in that program opposed the phase-out [S5].

The bill's own requirement for a GAO study of how the first wage increases affect employment, prices, and small businesses reflects that Congress itself acknowledged uncertainty about the law's economic effects [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: millions of the lowest-paid workers would see their hourly pay rise, and the increases arrive gradually over six years, which gives employers time to adjust. The honest costs are real but contested — economists disagree about how many jobs a $15 floor would cost, with the risk concentrated on the youngest and least experienced workers in low-cost regions. Phasing in the increase and indexing it to the median wage afterward is a reasonable design that limits the shock, though the bill offers no small-business or regional carve-out.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill 231-199, but the Senate simply placed it on its calendar and never brought it to a vote, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The House Committee on Education and Labor reported the bill on July 11, 2019, by a 28-20 vote [S7].
The House passed the bill on July 18, 2019 by a recorded vote of 231-199 [S8].
A Republican motion to recommit — which would have sent the bill back to committee with instructions to add a small-business exemption — failed 210-218 the same day [S7].
The Senate received the bill and placed it on its calendar under General Orders on July 22, 2019, but no vote was ever scheduled [S7].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the Senate ever voting on the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers paying wages below $15 — particularly large restaurant and retail chains and users of the tipped and disability subminimums — avoided the wage increase entirely, since a bill with majority support in the House died without the Senate ever voting on it.

for.name: Bobby Scott
for.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and guided it through his committee, which reported it 28-20.

for.name: House Democrats (228 members)
for.what_they_did: Voted nearly unanimously to pass the bill, 228 in favor with 6 opposed.

for.name: Nancy Pelosi
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the House floor for a vote under a rule permitting a motion to recommit.

for.name: 205 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar.

against.name: 192 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against passage, 192 of them, and offered the failed motion to recommit seeking a small-business exemption.

against.name: Rep. John Meuser
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add a small-business survival exemption; the motion failed 210-218.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split sharply by party: 228 of 234 Democrats voted yes while only 3 of 195 voting Republicans did, and no Senate Republican leader moved the bill after House passage.
